sections.title: Nomenclature and classification
sections.text: Megacollybia platyphylla (Pers.) Kotl. & Pouzar is the name accepted by Index Fungorum; its basionym is Agaricus platyphyllus Pers. (1796). Historical names include Collybia platyphylla, Tricholomopsis platyphylla, and Oudemansiella platyphylla. The consulted databases do not agree on family placement: Index Fungorum leaves the family unresolved within Agaricales, while NCBI places the taxon in Porotheleaceae.

sections.title: Cap, gills and stem
sections.text: The cap is usually 4–12 cm wide, grey-brown to olive-brown, darker at the centre, dry and marked by radial fibrils; its margin can split with age. The gills are white then cream, very broad and spaced to subdistant, sometimes joined by cross-veins; they are attached to the stem or notched, rather than free. The pale, fibrous stem, often 5–15 cm long, has no ring and bears white mycelial cords at its base, sometimes extending through buried wood. The whitish flesh is relatively thin, and the spore print is white.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This is a saprotroph of dead wood, especially broadleaf wood. Mycelial cords can connect the stem to buried wood, making the mushroom appear to grow directly from soil or leaf litter. In Europe, fruit bodies appear from spring to autumn, often from late spring into November depending on climate. The name was historically applied to closely related North American Megacollybia; taxonomic studies distinguish those species from M. platyphylla sensu stricto, which is known in Europe and as far as southwestern Siberia.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: Consumption is discouraged: the German Mycological Society notes occasional gastrointestinal complaints, and a North American Mycological Association toxicology report records a professionally confirmed case of vomiting and diarrhea after raw consumption. This report does not show that every specimen causes poisoning, but it does not support treating the species as edible. This entry is not an identification guide for consumption.

traits: Grey-brown to olive-brown cap with radial fibrils, often splitting at the margin as it ages
White to cream gills, very broad and spaced to subdistant, attached or notched, sometimes cross-veined
Pale, fibrous stem (often 5–15 cm), without a ring; white mycelial cords at the base connect with buried wood
Saprotroph of dead wood, especially broadleaf wood; fruit bodies may appear to emerge from soil
Occasional gastrointestinal complaints are reported; consumption is discouraged
safetyNote: Consumption is discouraged: gastrointestinal complaints are reported, including a NAMA case of vomiting and diarrhea after raw consumption with professional identification. Reports do not establish that every specimen has the same effect. Do not eat a mushroom identified from this entry.
